intro: Industrial engineers make production faster, cheaper and safer, skills that management and process roles reward. The closest of the 25 careers below is Industrial Production Managers, with an 81% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $126,060, which is 23% more than the $102,440 industrial engineers earn.
why_it_works: Improving a process means studying how people, machines and materials move, then redesigning the flow and proving it works. O*NET rates complex problem solving at 3.88 out of 5 for this job, and systems analysis and evaluation at 3.25. Production management, logistics and materials science use the same thinking. Almost every match needs no new degree. The gaps are quality checks and equipment maintenance.
tips: Plant management is the natural step: show results such as throughput, scrap or cost savings.
Materials Scientists earn $117,790, which is 15% more, and are a 78% match.
Database Architects earn $139,500, or 36% more, if you enjoy the data side of process work.

faq.q: What jobs can former industrial engineers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Industrial Production Managers (81%), Logistics Engineers (79%) and Materials Scientists (78%), based on O*NET 31.0. Quality Control Systems Managers are also 76% matched, with a median of $126,060 for their broader BLS group.

faq.q: Which careers for industrial engineers pay more?
faq.a: 8 of the 25 matches pay more than $102,440. Architectural and engineering managers earn $171,270 (67% more), Medical Dosimetrists $147,470 (44% more) and Database Architects $139,500 (36% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Engineering management usually needs a graduate degree.

faq.q: Do industrial engineers need another degree?
faq.a: Rarely. 24 of the 25 matches need no more education than industrial engineers already have, including all of the top 10. A bachelor's degree is the norm, held by 74% of workers in a close match, so your project results matter most.

faq.q: What skills should industrial engineers learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are quality control analysis, equipment maintenance, operations analysis and time management. Coordination already rates 3.12 out of 5 for industrial engineers in O*NET, so hands-on quality and maintenance knowledge is the main step toward plant leadership.
